messages.author: f2777afe52b659e4
messages.subject: Occupancy vs. DS ?
parts:
Hi all,

I have a question for you:

Several methods exist to compute detectability, e.g. DS (Distance Sampling),
Capture-Mark-Recapture (CMR) and Occupancy (software PRESENCE).

I see a lot of effort re. Occupancy, and which deal mostly just with
presence/absence (I am aware of the new efforts to handle continuous data).

I believe that getting at populations, densities, is a key goal though for
good species management etc.
So I am not so clear really how to go from pres/abs, occupancy, to
densities, e.g. from DS, or to link and assess both.

My real question is about the following:

Occupancy is inherently aspatial, it's usually just a POINT ESTIMATE, and
thus, 1 dimensional (strictly speaking: the tip of a needle). There is no
area for this at all.

In DS, we have AREA included (2 dimensional), and deal with detection width
or detection radius.
We also know that such detection widths are inherently NOT constant, and
ought to be modeled (e.g. declining detection function, dynamic changes).

Assigning 'just an area estimate' to a sighting is a rather critical factor
for any valid density estimation, right ?

So how can Occupancy and DS truly be compared ?
And if it cannot, what does that mean ?

I see applications where Occupancies get obtained for areas (e.g. plots,
squares), but how can that really be valid for true density estimates ?
Doesn't DS teach us otherwise: Any centimeter counts, not ?
(try it out with your own data and when you start to extrapolate to larger
areas and landscapes)

Isn't the same problem true for CMR as well ?

I would welcome any thoughts and ideas about this.

Thanks in advance; very best

F.

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: Occupancy vs. DS ?
parts:
Occupancy simply converts abundance to 0/1 and can be defined for an
area although I'm not sure it always is in applications. It uses
multiple visits or multiple methods with some fairly strong assumptions
to assess detection probability. Usually requires 5-6 visits. I can
see it working well for relatively sedentary critters like amphibians,
or territorial birds and with well-defined or possibly discrete sites
(e.g, ponds).

--jeff
